title: Republicans Prove Why Money Can’t Fix Losing Campaigns
text:
Supported by
Guest Essay
More Cash Is Not What Republicans Needed
When it comes to facing voters, it seems as though politicians live by the words of Berry Gordy and Janie Bradford’s unforgettable song “Money (That’s What I Want)”:
Your love give me such a thrill
But your love don’t pay my bills
I need money! That’s what I want!
Despite record spending across the board this year — in Senate general election advertising alone, Republicans outspent Democrats by $250 million — Republicans lost big. The old assumption that big money always wins elections was smashed just as thoroughly as the Republican majorities in both the House and the Senate.
Money does count; have no doubt. What is easy to miss but political consultants in both parties know and quietly whisper to one another is that while tons of money can powerfully amplify a great campaign message, it cannot alone create one.
All campaigns are starved for resources; there is never enough time, funding or, usually, luck. Campaigns are expensive. Paid advertising is costly. Staff members need to get at least starvation wages. Experienced consultants don’t work for cheap.
Think for a minute like a campaign manager. Here’s the kind of daily team discussion you will hear in a major race: “Should the candidate do a live six-minute interview tonight on the top Detroit station and reach over 100,000 viewers — but it would mean canceling the first of the three fund-raising events we have planned? A new tracking poll shows we’re in trouble in Grand Rapids; get the candidate there and blow up tomorrow in Flint … but that means blowing off a long-promised live interview with the touchy supreme podcaster Liberty Gazoo, and Gazoo will be really angry. OK, then we’ll just charter a plane to Grand Rapids! A charter is $9,000, but we are low on cash and the media buy has to go out by noon today?”
That is why campaign teams crave ever more money: Almost every decision involves a painful allocation of scare resources, so the obvious problem-solving tool is to get more funding.
This psychological factor — the campaign finance version of FOMO — cannot be overstated. It’s why no campaign team has ever lost sleep after spending more money. In those fearful, last days of a campaign who can say no to that last 116 thousand in get-out-the-vote spend?
